misconceptions.statement: Heavy objects sink and light objects float.
misconceptions.why: Everyday examples like a stone versus a leaf link weight directly to sinking.
misconceptions.fix: Whether something floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not its weight alone; a huge heavy log floats while a small pin sinks.

probe.question: A big wooden log weighs 50 kg and a small iron nail weighs 5 g. Which sinks in water?
probe.wrong_answer: The log, because it is much heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible property decides the whole outcome
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about floating and sinking

misconceptions.statement: An object either floats or sinks as a fixed property, whatever liquid it is put in.
misconceptions.why: Students mostly see objects only in water and treat floating as a label on the object.
misconceptions.fix: Floating depends on the object's density relative to the liquid; an egg sinks in fresh water but floats in strong salt water.

probe.question: An egg sinks in plain water. What happens in very salty water?
probe.wrong_answer: It still sinks, because eggs are sinking objects.

misconceptions.root_belief: properties belong to the object, not the situation

misconceptions.statement: Density and weight mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: In daily speech 'heavy' and 'dense' are used loosely for the same idea.
misconceptions.fix: Density is mass per unit volume; weight is the pull of gravity on the whole object, so a big object can be heavy but not dense.

probe.question: Is a 1 kg cotton pile as dense as a 1 kg iron ball?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are 1 kg so their density is the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: related terms are interchangeable
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of density concept development in school students

misconceptions.statement: A small piece of a material has lower density than a large piece of the same material.
misconceptions.why: Students link density to total amount, so a smaller amount seems less dense.
misconceptions.fix: Density is the same for any amount of a pure material because mass and volume shrink together.

probe.question: A large iron block is cut in half. How does the density of one half compare with the whole?
probe.wrong_answer: It is half as dense.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of intensive versus extensive quantities in density

misconceptions.statement: Any object with a density number bigger than water's will float.
misconceptions.why: Students think a bigger number always means better or higher up.
misconceptions.fix: Water is 1 g/cm3; objects with density greater than 1 sink and those with less than 1 float.

probe.question: Iron has density 7.8 g/cm3 and water 1 g/cm3. Does iron float?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 7.8 is bigger than 1.

misconceptions.root_belief: a bigger number means a bigger outcome

misconceptions.statement: Objects float only if they contain air.
misconceptions.why: Air-filled things like balls and tubes are the common floaters seen.
misconceptions.fix: Anything less dense than the liquid floats, including solid wax and solid wood with no air pockets noticed.

probe.question: Why does a solid piece of wax float on water?
probe.wrong_answer: It must have air trapped inside it.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Water does not push upward; only gravity acts on an object in water.
misconceptions.why: Students cannot see the upward push, only the downward weight they feel.
misconceptions.fix: Liquids push up on any object placed in them; this upward force is called upthrust or buoyant force.

probe.question: What forces act on a cork held under water and let go?
probe.wrong_answer: Only its weight, pulling it down.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about forces in fluids

misconceptions.statement: Upthrust acts only on floating objects; a sinking stone has no upthrust.
misconceptions.why: Upthrust is linked with the idea of staying up, so sinking seems to mean none.
misconceptions.fix: Every object in a liquid feels upthrust; a stone sinks because its weight is greater than the upthrust.

probe.question: A stone sinks in water. Is there an upthrust on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, upthrust only works on things that float.

misconceptions.root_belief: a force exists only when its effect is seen
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about forces in water

misconceptions.statement: For an object to float, upthrust must be greater than its weight.
misconceptions.why: Students think extra upward force is needed to hold something up against gravity.
misconceptions.fix: A floating object is at rest, so upthrust exactly equals its weight; upthrust larger than weight would make it rise.

probe.question: A boat floats steadily. How does the upthrust compare to its weight?
probe.wrong_answer: Upthrust is greater than the weight.

misconceptions.root_belief: staying still needs a winning force

misconceptions.statement: The deeper an object is pushed under water, the greater the upthrust on it.
misconceptions.why: Students know pressure increases with depth and carry this over to upthrust.
misconceptions.fix: Once fully under water, upthrust stays the same at any depth because the displaced volume does not change.

probe.question: A fully submerged ball is pushed deeper. What happens to the upthrust?
probe.wrong_answer: It increases.

misconceptions.root_belief: going further in increases the effect
misconceptions.source_hint: concept inventories on buoyancy and fluid pressure

misconceptions.statement: A heavier object gets a bigger upthrust than a lighter one.
misconceptions.why: Students think a bigger load needs a bigger supporting force in every case.
misconceptions.fix: Upthrust depends on the volume of liquid displaced and the liquid's density, not on the object's weight.

probe.question: A 1 kg steel ball and a 1 kg wooden ball of the same size are fully under water. Which has more upthrust?
probe.wrong_answer: The steel ball, as it is heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: heavy things dominate every interaction

misconceptions.statement: Upthrust on an object is always equal to the object's own weight.
misconceptions.why: Floating objects are the usual example, where the two are equal, and students overgeneralise.
misconceptions.fix: Upthrust equals the weight of the liquid displaced; it equals the object's weight only when the object floats.

probe.question: A 5 N stone is fully under water and displaces 2 N of water. What is the upthrust?

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case is the general rule

misconceptions.statement: A floating object always displaces water equal to its whole volume.
misconceptions.why: Students link displacement with the object's total size from sinking-stone experiments.
misconceptions.fix: A floating object displaces only as much water as its submerged part; the volume above the surface displaces nothing.

probe.question: A block of volume 100 cm3 floats with 60 cm3 under water. How much water does it displace?

misconceptions.root_belief: the part behaves like the whole

misconceptions.statement: An object feels lighter in water because water reduces its mass.
misconceptions.why: Students use mass and weight loosely and see a smaller reading on the balance.
misconceptions.fix: Mass does not change; the object seems lighter because upthrust acts upward and reduces the force needed to hold it.

probe.question: A spring balance reading falls when a stone is dipped in water. What changed?
probe.wrong_answer: The stone's mass became less.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of mass versus weight confusion

misconceptions.statement: Dissolved salt disappears in water, so salt water has the same density as fresh water.
misconceptions.why: The salt cannot be seen after dissolving, so students think it adds nothing.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved salt adds mass without much extra volume, so salt water is denser than fresh water.

probe.question: Is a litre of salt solution heavier than a litre of pure water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the salt has vanished so they are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on conservation of matter in dissolving

misconceptions.statement: Things float in the Dead Sea because its water is thick like syrup.
misconceptions.why: The word dense is understood in daily speech as thick or sticky.
misconceptions.fix: Dense means more mass per unit volume; Dead Sea water has so much dissolved salt that it is denser than a person's body.

probe.question: Why is it easy to float in the Dead Sea?
probe.wrong_answer: Its water is thicker and stickier.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A floating object sinks to the same depth in fresh water and salt water.
misconceptions.why: Students think the object alone decides how much of it is under water.
misconceptions.fix: In denser salt water less volume is needed to displace the object's weight, so it floats higher.

probe.question: A ship moves from a river into the sea. How does its depth in the water change?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays at the same depth.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the object matters, not the surroundings

misconceptions.statement: A steel ship floats because steel is lighter than water.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the material's property to the ship and ignore its shape.
misconceptions.fix: Steel is denser than water; a ship floats because its hollow shape makes its average density less than water's.

probe.question: Why does a steel ship float when a steel nail sinks?
probe.wrong_answer: Ship steel is lighter than the nail's steel.

misconceptions.root_belief: the part's property decides the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on floating and shape of objects

misconceptions.statement: Loading cargo onto a floating ship does not change how deep it sits in water.
misconceptions.why: Students think a floating object has already found its level.
misconceptions.fix: More cargo means more weight, so the ship must displace more water and sinks deeper until upthrust again equals weight.

probe.question: A ship takes on a lot of cargo. What happens to the part under water?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: floating is a fixed state

misconceptions.statement: A submarine dives only because its propellers push it downward.
misconceptions.why: Moving vehicles are assumed to need engine power for every motion.
misconceptions.fix: A submarine fills ballast tanks with water to become denser than the surrounding water and sink, and empties them with air to rise.

probe.question: How does a stationary submarine sink?
probe.wrong_answer: Its propellers push it down.

misconceptions.root_belief: movement always needs an active push

misconceptions.statement: Heating air makes it lighter because its particles lose mass.
misconceptions.why: Students see less weight effect and think the matter itself shrinks.
misconceptions.fix: Heated air expands so the same space holds fewer particles; the particles keep their mass but the air becomes less dense.

probe.question: Why is hot air in a balloon lighter than the same volume of cold air?
probe.wrong_answer: Its particles lose mass when heated.

misconceptions.root_belief: changing a property changes the stuff itself

misconceptions.statement: A hot air balloon rises because gravity stops acting on it.
misconceptions.why: Seeing something go up against gravity suggests gravity has disappeared.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity still acts; the balloon rises because upthrust from the surrounding air is greater than its total weight.

probe.question: Is there gravity on a hot air balloon that is rising?
probe.wrong_answer: No, gravity does not act on it any more.

misconceptions.root_belief: upward motion means no downward force
misconceptions.source_hint: research on gravity and upward motion misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: Buoyancy and Archimedes' principle work only in liquids, not in air.
misconceptions.why: Textbook examples are all in water, so students think only liquids push upward.
misconceptions.fix: Air is a fluid and also gives upthrust equal to the weight of air displaced, which is why balloons rise.

probe.question: Does air exert any upthrust on a helium balloon?
probe.wrong_answer: No, upthrust happens only in liquids.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule only applies where first learned
